answers.justification: The drop is limited to floors 6-8 and to room comfort (E2). Those floors' scores fall on 5-20 Aug and recover once CH-2 is fixed (E4, E3, C6), heat accounts for 56 of 74 negative comments (E4), and room-temperature complaints at the desk went from 1 to 24 (E5).
Check-in scores are flat (E2), kiosk complaints and comments slightly fell (E4, E5), queues got shorter (E5), kiosk availability was 99.6% (C3), and front-office staffing was stable (C2).
Cleanliness scores are steady on both floor blocks (E2), inspection pass rates are 95-96% (E5), and cleanliness comments did not rise (E4, C4); the 'dusty' review also complained of heat (C4).
The questionnaire, invitation method, timing and response rates did not change (E2, C5), and floors 1-5 were stable over the same period (E2, E4).

On floors 1-5, value for money fell 0.3 while the overall score fell only 0.1, which is within normal variation (E2). The Revenue Manager cannot separate the rate rise from the usual August seasonal dip (E6, C11), so any contribution is unestablished.
The timing matches (E3, C6, E4), the mechanism is clear (chiller trip leading to 26.5-29 C rooms, E3), floors 1-5 act as a control group (E2), and scores recovered after the repair (E4).
The kiosks went live in June but July's score was 8.6, check-in scores and complaints did not change (E2, E5), and the kiosks worked reliably (C3).
The rate rise came at the same time as the drop in value scores (E2, C11), but the usual seasonal August dip (E6) is a confounder that has not been ruled out.
Cleanliness ratings did not fall after the contractor changed (8.7 to 8.7 on floors 1-5, 8.7 to 8.6 on floors 6-8, E2), inspection pass rates held (E5), and cleanliness comments were flat (E4).
The deferred preventive service and the missing spare part caused the 11-day outage (E3, C12, C15), and CH-1 is the same model, the same age and also overdue (C15).
No evidence shows that Orrin's quality declined (E2, E5, C1, C10), so serving notice would punish the wrong party for an engineering failure.
There is no evidence yet that the rate rise caused the value drop rather than the seasonal dip (E6, C11), and rates can be changed at any time, so there is no rush (E6).
All 517 affected stays already received a written apology and a half-night credit (E5, C7), so another apology with a return-stay offer is reasonable but adds less than A1.
The floor 6-8 responses are valid feedback from a real failure (E2, E4, C5), so leaving them out of a bonus-linked score would hide information.
The evidence pins the cause on the CH-2 outage with deferred maintenance behind it (E2-E4, C6, C12, C15), which is enough to commit to A1.

ambiguousItems: Q13 (A4): the affected guests were already given an apology and a credit, so a second outreach could reasonably be rated 'acceptable' or 'preferred' (a return-stay offer for loyalty recovery).
Q8 (R3): 'association-only' vs 'unknown', because the value-score drop could be entirely seasonal (E6).
Q5 (H5): 'unknown' vs 'supported', because on floors 1-5 the value score fell 0.3, more than the 0.2 normal-variation band and more than last year's 0.2 seasonal dip (E2, E6).
caseProblems: Minor: 96 floor 6-8 responses from 517 stays checking out 5-20 Aug is about 19%, below the stated 30% response rate (C5). This is plausible (missing emails, upset guests) but not explained.
C7 largely repeats the outage-recovery details already given in E5 (517 stays, half-night credit).

No catalogue title gives away the answer, but most of the decisive evidence (E2-E5) is already in the initial evidence, so the catalogue adds little that discriminates beyond confirmation (C6, C12, C15).

rulings.explanation: E5 says every affected floor 6-8 stay (all 517 checking out 5-20 August) already received a written apology and a half-night goodwill credit at checkout. A4 would therefore repeat a recovery step that has already been taken, and it only deals with past harm. The best next actions are those that address what is still exposed. E3 shows deferred maintenance on both chillers, no spare part, and CH-1 still unserviced. A1 targets that confirmed cause and the risk of a repeat; A4 does nothing about it. So A4 is not 'among the best next actions' and 'preferred' cannot be defended. It is low-risk and plausibly helps loyalty, so it is not 'harmful'. It does not depend on any unconfirmed hypothesis, so it is not 'premature'. That leaves 'acceptable' as the only defensible rating. The flag's argument that a second outreach could be 'preferred' for loyalty recovery overlooks the fact that the main recovery has already been delivered.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional hardening: add a line to E5 or E4 saying that no follow-up loyalty or retention issue has been flagged among the affected guests. That would further close off a 'preferred' reading.

rulings.explanation: The task defines 'unknown' as evidence that is 'insufficient even to show association', and 'association-only' as cases where the two conditions 'co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established'. The evidence documents the co-occurrence directly. Rates rose 6% from 1 August (E6). Value for money fell in August (E2), by 0.3 on floors 1-5, which is above the 0.2 noise band. Price/value comments rose from 2 to 6, with 4 of them from floors 1-5 (E4). It is true that the drop could be entirely seasonal (E6), but that point only stops the link from being called causal. It does not erase the documented co-occurrence. Nothing counts against the link, so 'contradicted' does not fit, and the confound rules out 'causal'. Under the stated semantics, 'association-only' is the only fit.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional: state in the edge semantics that a single-period co-occurrence that a confound could fully explain still counts as association-only. That would remove any lingering pull toward 'unknown'.

rulings.explanation: H5 is a claim about the overall score, not the value-for-money subscore. On floors 1-5, the only block not confounded by the outage, the overall score fell 0.1 (E2). That is inside the 0.2 normal-variation band and the same as last August's 0.1 overall dip with no rate change (E6). The flag points to the 0.3 value-for-money drop, but last year's seasonal value dip was 0.2, so the excess is only 0.1. That is below the vendor's noise threshold. The revenue manager also says explicitly that nothing separates the rate effect from the seasonal one (E6). 'Supported' would require evidence that favours H5 over the seasonal rival, and the evidence does not provide that. On the other hand, a movement within the noise band is consistent with a small contribution, so 'contradicted' is not warranted either. 'Unknown' is the only defensible answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional: in E6, add last year's floor-level value-for-money change if it was available, or reword H5 to say 'contributed to the drop in the overall score' explicitly as distinct from the value subscore. Either would stop readers conflating the 0.3 subscore drop with the overall-score claim.
